claims.text: Boride-based substrates used in hot-dip aluminum plating are susceptible to attack by molten aluminum.
A dense Al2O3 coating approximately 10–20 µm thick can be deposited on the boride-based substrate by plasma spraying.
An optimized interlayer or pretreatment improves adhesion of the plasma-sprayed Al2O3 coating.
An optimized interlayer or pretreatment reduces residual stresses in the coating.
Controlled plasma spraying at moderate substrate temperatures, together with an interlayer, produces a uniform and defect-minimized Al2O3 barrier.
The resulting Al2O3 layer can remain adherent and microstructurally sound during conditions representative of hot-dip aluminum plating.
A continuous Al2O3 barrier prevents direct contact between molten aluminum and the underlying boride surface.
Al2O3 has a high melting point.
Al2O3 is chemically inert enough toward molten aluminum to resist chemical attack under hot-dip plating conditions.
The Al2O3 coating physically blocks molten aluminum from attacking the boride-based substrate.
Improved interlayer adhesion minimizes coating microcracking during thermal cycling and prolonged exposure.
Maintaining coating integrity during thermal cycling preserves the barrier against molten-aluminum corrosion.
An interlayer-enhanced, plasma-sprayed Al2O3 coating will significantly reduce molten-aluminum corrosion rate relative to an untreated boride surface.
Reducing the molten-aluminum corrosion rate will extend the service life of boride-based hot-dip plating components.
Inadequate interlayer adhesion can compromise the corrosion-protection performance of the coating.
Improper plasma-spraying parameters can compromise the corrosion-protection performance of the coating.
Thermal cycling beyond the coating's design limits can compromise its corrosion-protection performance.
The magnitude of corrosion reduction depends on coating thickness, interlayer effectiveness, and operating conditions.
